newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Unions show more support for Serbian opposition.
newsitem.headline: Unions show more support for Serbian opposition.

text.p: Serbia's biggest trade union organisation broke new ground on Monday to offer cautious support to a smaller independent union's protests against President Slobodan Milosevic's socialists.

The Alliance of Independent Trade Unions, a traditionally pro-government group, gave public support to Nezavisnost, the first union to join the protests, but stopped short of calling its own members out on the steets.

Nezavisnost workers, protesting about pay and workers' rights and conditions, have joined students and the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition in a wave of protest across Serbia over Milosevic's refusal to recognise local election results.
"Nezavisnost's demands are justified. What they are doing is a legitimate form of trade union activity," Dragan Radulovic, president of the alliance's council said.
The Alliance has stayed out of the conflict so far, saying it feared its workers' specific grievances would be submerged by the opposition's political agenda.
Workers said privately they supported the groundswell of anti-Milosevic feeling but would not march behind their own banners for fear of being sacked.
"Yugoslav trade unionism doesn't have enough of a tradition in mass rallies of this kind and is a relatively young movement in Serbia and Montenegro," one union leader said.

The annulment of elections, denying the opposition victory in Belgrade and other towns in Serbia, brought a record 200,000 people out in rallies in Belgrade at the weekend, the latest in the daily protests that have lasted since mid-November.

Nezavisnost, with about 80,000 members, plans to protest on Tuesday outside the Serbian parliament which is due to discuss several draft laws on labour and employment which workers believe will harm their interests.
Most of Serbia's state-controlled industry has still not recovered from being idled by 3-1/2 years of U.N. sanctions and many workers do little or nothing while at their posts.
Workers should receive 60 percent of their wages during compulsory layoffs but cash-strapped authorities have failed to make regular payments, prompting increasing demands for backpay.

Grozdana Miljanovic, secretary of the Alliance's council, said official statistics put the number of employed workers in Yugoslavia at 2.4 million but independent institutes say only between 700,000 and 800,000 are actually working.
The government plans to abolish the compulsory leave system from January 1 in a move which could cost 800,000 jobs.

"The trade union will insist that the state begin an active employment policy," Miljanovic said. "We cannot accept workers finding themselves on the streets or outside unemployment offices. They are not the ones to blame for the catastrophic economic situation."
